title: Inverse-Root Support and Fourier Fusion for Polynomial Exponential Periods
oneLine: Relative to named primitive-monodromy and finite-projective-group classifications, an unrefereed successor classifies every complex polynomial phase of fixed-seed cyclic rank at most three and every proper rank-preserving outer extension.
abstract: For a complex polynomial phase P, the cyclic rank generated by the fixed seed dx equals the nonzero residue-channel count of the normalised inverse series at infinity and the reduced constant span dimension of the generic inverse roots. This anonymous, unrefereed successor builds on that bridge and the previously published Fourier law for block fusion to give an all-degree classification for cyclic rank at most three, relative to named results on primitive polynomial monodromy and finite projective linear groups. Up to affine equivalence and lower-rank intersections, the list consists of powers, Dickson polynomials, quadratic- and cubic-over-power phases, indecomposable quartics, and one degree-twelve quartic collision. The candidate also classifies every proper rank-preserving outer extension: power towers, aligned Dickson towers, one aligned square of an odd-centred cubic-over-power phase, and one cubic extension of the exceptional quartic. The proof closes the inherited root-span interface, replaces an analytic boundedness step by invariant-integral finite-pole and infinity-order descent, supplies a full-block stabiliser lemma, audits all primitive factors, repairs a false uniform Kummer-kernel assertion by coefficient strata, and treats arbitrary mixed Dickson chains through a direct invariant-field argument. Sixteen Lean theorem controls, two separate producer-side CAS implementations, semantic negative controls, and two internal model-assisted specialist re-audits support the package. They do not establish complete formalisation, unaffiliated reproduction, external specialist review, peer review, correctness of the imported classifications, or priority.
narration: A polynomial exponential period begins with a polynomial phase and an integral. Differentiate that integral repeatedly, and a differential system appears. The fixed-seed cyclic rank asks how much of that system is generated by one starting form, dx. Earlier releases showed that this rank can be read at infinity: normalise an inverse branch of the polynomial, split its Laurent series into congruence channels, and count the nonzero channels. The same number is the dimension of the reduced constant span of the polynomial's inverse roots. A Fourier formula then explains how those root spans fuse when the polynomial decomposes. Version zero point six takes the next step. Relative to named classification theorems for primitive polynomial monodromy and finite projective linear groups, the candidate classifies every complex polynomial phase whose fixed-seed cyclic rank is at most three, in every degree. Up to affine equivalence and lower-rank overlaps, the list contains powers, Dickson polynomials, quadratic and cubic polynomials over a power, indecomposable quartics, and one exceptional degree-twelve collision. It also identifies every proper outer composition that preserves rank. Powers extend through power towers. Dickson polynomials extend inside one aligned dihedral tower. An odd-centred cubic over a power admits one aligned square. The exceptional quartic admits one cubic collision. No other proper rank-preserving outer extension survives the argument. Several missing interfaces had to be closed. An algebraic invariant-integral descent replaces an analytic boundedness step. A full-block stabiliser lemma connects block fusion to absolute monodromy. A source-exact audit reduces the primitive cases to powers, Dickson factors, and quartics. A false draft claim about a uniform Kummer kernel was found on a special even-exponent coefficient stratum; the release preserves the counterexample and replaces the claim with a stratified theorem and exceptional descent. Arbitrary mixed Dickson chains are handled directly through the invariant field of the full outer polynomial. The old degree-twenty atlas and the preregistered degree-thirty-two experiment remain useful regression and bridge evidence, but neither is extrapolated into the universal proof. Producer-side checks include sixteen Lean theorem controls, ten exact global computer-algebra checks, nineteen repaired Kummer checks, thirteen adversarial receipt mutations in each Python mode, clean-archive replay, and two internal model-assisted specialist re-audits. These are serious controls, but they are not external peer review. The imported classification theorems are not reproved, the Lean development is deliberately partial, and no unaffiliated researcher has rerun or reimplemented the package. Novelty and priority searches are bounded rather than exhaustive. Why might this matter? The classification converts an unbounded search through polynomial coefficients and decomposition chains into a short structural decision tree. Researchers can read rank from inverse support, test whether a decomposition preserves rank through projected support and block fusion, and rule out every outer extension not on the four-item list. That makes the package useful both as a theorem candidate and as a benchmark for independent computer algebra, formalisation, and future work on differential-equation order. The scholarly creator is Anonymous; Ian Pitchford is the repository maintainer and publisher. This briefing is a communication aid, not additional mathematical evidence.

problem.name: Fixed-seed cyclicity for polynomial exponential periods

keyResults: For every complex polynomial P of degree at least two, the fixed-seed cyclic rank equals both the nonzero inverse-at-infinity residue-channel count and the reduced constant inverse-root-span dimension.

Relative to named primitive-polynomial-monodromy and finite-projective-group classifications, every complex polynomial phase of cyclic rank at most three is affine-equivalent to a power, Dickson polynomial, quadratic- or cubic-over-power phase, indecomposable quartic, or the degree-twelve quartic collision, with lower-rank intersections removed.

Every proper rank-preserving outer extension is a power tower, an aligned Dickson tower, the aligned square of an odd-centred cubic-over-power phase, or the cubic extension of the exceptional quartic; the two rank-three extensions cannot repeat.

Invariant-integral descent proves the required finite-pole and infinity-order bounds, while the full-block stabiliser lemma supplies the missing interface between full fusion and absolute block monodromy.
A false full-Kummer-kernel draft claim on B nonzero, A squared equal to 4B, and even exponent is replaced by a coefficient-stratified theorem and exceptional-stratum descent.
A direct rational-function invariant-field argument classifies arbitrary mixed Dickson chains without extrapolating from the bounded Dickson regression grid.

The 1,152-case degree-twenty atlas and preregistered degree-thirty-two experiment remain bounded regression and bridge evidence; the all-degree result rests on the written structural proof relative to its named imports.

This establishes strong producer-side consistency, replay and availability, not independent theorem verification.
